svg.aria-label: How to write ி, நன்றி: 6 parts, ி, ந, ன, ், ற, ி, one after another
svg.title: Writing ி, நன்றி
svg.desc: 6 parts written one after another: ி, ந, ன, ், ற, ி (tamil). The parts are in the order the hand writes them, which is not always the order they are typed: a vowel sign written to the left of its consonant comes before it. Each vowel sign is drawn on its own, without the consonant it attaches to. Each part has its own group of frames; frame N of a group shows movements 1 to N of that part, the movement being added drawn in ink over the finished part, whose outline is read from _fonts/NotoSansTamil-Static.ttf. Each part is drawn at its own scale from its own cited stroke order, so the strip does not show how large the parts are next to each other, how far apart they sit, or any join between them. Stroke order: ி: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Tamil recognizer, class 37 (ி, i sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native Tamil writers (MIT licence, 2012) <https://lipitk.sourceforge.net/lipi-reco.htm>; ந: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 5, ந (University of Texas at Austin), p. 193 <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>; ன: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 13, ன (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 195 <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>; ்: Abhinaya Rajarajan, Varai (Swift Student Challenge 2026), reference drawings recorded by hand for the 18 Tamil consonants with pulli, க் to ன் (repository commit 952294fa, no licence: facts only) <https://github.com/abhinayaRajarajan/varai>; ற: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 10, ற (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 194 <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>; ி: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Tamil recognizer, class 37 (ி, i sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native Tamil writers (MIT licence, 2012) <https://lipitk.sourceforge.net/lipi-reco.htm>. Source notes on variation: ி: The recognizer stores native Tamil writers' tablet pen traces, each resampled to 60 points. 205 of the 206 stored prototypes of the i sign are one pen-down stroke. In 161 of those 205 the pen starts at the tip of the hook and first moves up; 200 turn clockwise, over the top to the right; 152 end at the foot of the stem. The traces are scaled to a square, so they fix the start, the direction and the pen lifts, not the proportions: the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline of the sign on its own. Handwriting varies by writer. ந: Module 5 identifies ந as the voiced dental nasal and notes that its extended final curve may be omitted. Appendix I Frame 5 numbers six hand-movements. Native writers draw them as one continuous stroke, and this ductus follows the six movements in order without lifting: the pen climbs back up the middle upright to where the right bowl leaves it. In HP Labs India's online Tamil handwriting data (the LipiTk 4.0 Tamil isolated-character recognizer, trained on hpl-tamil-iso-char), 85% of the 224 stored prototypes of ந are a single pen-down stroke. Tamil handwriting varies by school; this is one attested order fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline. ன: Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation; there is no single national stroke-order standard. Appendix I Frame 13 numbers six hand-movements for ன. Native writers draw them as one continuous stroke, and this ductus follows the six movements in order without lifting: the top bar runs out to the right edge, so the pen comes back along it to the right upright and draws the upright down. In HP Labs India's online Tamil handwriting data (the LipiTk 4.0 Tamil isolated-character recognizer, trained on hpl-tamil-iso-char), 94% of the 335 stored prototypes of ன are a single pen-down stroke. ்: One writer's recorded reference drawings, stored in the order they were drawn. In all 18 the consonant body is one stroke and the puḷḷi is a separate second stroke, made after the body is complete, so it costs one pen lift. Its centre sits above the body at 0.47 to 0.65 of the body's width (0.54 for க்). An earlier reading of Info-farmer's Writing Tamil animations of the consonants on Wikimedia Commons, which show each consonant with its puḷḷi, also places the dot after the body. Confidence is medium: one recorded writer, and only stroke count, order and the dot's bounding box were read; the dot is about 10 by 13 canvas units, too small to say which way the pen moved, so the short downward dab drawn here is not a claim. The path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil disc, which the font centres at 0.43 to 0.60 of the consonant's width, a little left of where this writer put it. Handwriting varies by writer. ற: Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation; there is no single national stroke-order standard. Appendix I Frame 10 numbers five hand-movements, with movement 3 on the middle upright beside movement 2. Native writers draw them as one continuous stroke, and this ductus follows the five movements in order without lifting. The bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline prints a single shared middle upright, so movement 3 climbs back up it to start the second arch. In HP Labs India's online Tamil handwriting data (the LipiTk 4.0 Tamil isolated-character recognizer, trained on hpl-tamil-iso-char), 99% of the 378 stored prototypes of ற are a single pen-down stroke. ி: The recognizer stores native Tamil writers' tablet pen traces, each resampled to 60 points. 205 of the 206 stored prototypes of the i sign are one pen-down stroke. In 161 of those 205 the pen starts at the tip of the hook and first moves up; 200 turn clockwise, over the top to the right; 152 end at the foot of the stem. The traces are scaled to a square, so they fix the start, the direction and the pen lifts, not the proportions: the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline of the sign on its own. Handwriting varies by writer.
svg.text: How it is written — 6 parts, one after another
Part 1 of 6 — one unbroken stroke · 3 movements
Part 2 of 6 — one unbroken stroke · 6 movements
Part 3 of 6 — one unbroken stroke · 6 movements
Part 5 of 6 — one unbroken stroke · 5 movements
Part 6 of 6 — one unbroken stroke · 3 movements
Parts 1 and 6: stroke order after HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Tamil recognizer, class 37 (ி, i sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from
Part 2: stroke order after Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 5, ந (University of Texas at Austin), p. 193
Part 3: stroke order after Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 13, ன (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 195
Part 4: stroke order after Abhinaya Rajarajan, Varai (Swift Student Challenge 2026), reference drawings recorded by hand for the 18 Tamil consonants with pulli, க் to ன் (repository
Part 5: stroke order after Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 10, ற (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 194
This order is attested, not standardised; the source records where it varies.
